main_damage_causes: Collapse of the opening Malfoy Manor walk-and-council scene, which is the primary characterisation vehicle for Yaxley in the book — his sardonic wit, competitive status-seeking, and most significant achievement (the Thicknesse Imperius) are all either cut or reassigned, reducing him from an established schemer to a named face at the table.

Systematic removal of Yaxley's ideological voice — his explicit blood-purity language, his jeering participation in the Muggle-born hearings, and his performative cruelty before an approving audience — which in the book distinguishes him as a true-believing bigot rather than a generic enforcer.

Loss of Yaxley's agency and credit across multiple scenes: his proud announcement of placing Thicknesse under Imperius, his near-deception by Harry's lie in the Atrium, his named defeat by George and Lee Jordan — small moments that collectively gave him definition and a complete arc across the two films.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Drawing Room meeting at Malfoy Manor
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Yaxley walks alongside Snape to Malfoy Manor, initiating conversation about being 'a little late,' commenting sardoni­cally on Lucius's peacocks ('He always did himself well, Lucius. Peacocks…'), and then at the table actively challenges Snape's intelligence about Harry's movement date, presents his own competing information about Dawlish, squares his shoulders to report his success placing an Imperius Curse on Pius Thicknesse, and eagerly pushes further ('We are at an advantage there, my Lord') to win some approval. He is a scheming, confident, status-hungry Death Eater who actively competes for Voldemort's favour.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Yaxley's arrival walk with Snape is entirely absent. He appears only as a face at the table who leans into the light to deliver two lines of intelligence about Dawlish and then says nothing more. His sardonic commentary on the peacocks is cut, his shoulder-squaring confidence is absent, his report on the Imperius Curse on Thicknesse is transferred: in the film it is Thicknesse himself who is present at the table (already under the curse) and Voldemort addresses him directly, so Yaxley's proud announcement of that achievement simply does not happen. His competitive bid for approval ('We are at an advantage there, my Lord') is also cut.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book opening chapter is almost entirely built around Yaxley as Snape's walking companion and as an active, ambitious participant in the war council. His personality — sardonic, status-hungry, eager to outshine Snape — is established through the walk, the peacock comment, and his repeated bids for Voldemort's favour. The film collapses him to a minor speaking presence at the table and reassigns his most significant achievement (placing Thicknesse under Imperius) to an implicit fait accompli. This strips the character of the defining traits the book gives him in his very first appearance and reduces him from a credible rival-schemer to a background Death Eater.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Ministry of Magic Atrium encounter with Cattermole/Ron
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Yaxley corners Cattermole/Ron and delivers a sustained, calculated act of cruelty: he uses his wife's blood-status hearing as a weapon ('your wife's Blood Status will be in even greater doubt'), explicitly invokes Mudblood slurs ('I assure you, the brats of Mudbloods do not stir our sympathies' and 'not that any woman I married would ever be mistaken for such filth'), gives a one-hour ultimatum, and parts with 'a nod and unpleasant smile to Harry' — expecting Harry-as-Runcorn to appreciate his bullying. This establishes his bigotry as calculated and performative, wielded as institutional power.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film version trims the exchange significantly. Yaxley confronts Ron/Cattermole about the rain, issues the threat about the wife's interrogation and the one-hour deadline, but the explicit Mudblood slurs ('brats of Mudbloods,' 'filth,' 'marry a pureblood next time') are entirely absent. The complicit nod to Harry/Runcorn is also cut. The scene ends with Yaxley storming off before the slur-laden extension of the threat that appears in the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this encounter to show that Yaxley's cruelty is not just functional intimidation but ideologically savoured — he takes pleasure in the language of blood purity and invites Runcorn to share in it. The film retains the threat but removes the ideological relish, making Yaxley a straightforward bureaucratic bully rather than a true-believing bigot who performs his racism for an audience. The complicit nod to Runcorn is a small but telling detail of how corruption operates in the Ministry, and its loss slightly flattens the scene's institutional horror.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Muggle-Born Registration Commission courtroom
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Yaxley sits on the raised platform beside Umbridge as a full co-prosecutor, laughs jeeringly at Umbridge's mockery of Mrs. Cattermole's parents being greengrocers, and is treated as a genuine threat — Harry specifically considers casting Muffliato on both Umbridge and Yaxley. When Harry stuns Umbridge, Yaxley reaches for his own wand but is immediately Stupefied by Harry before he can act. The book also has Yaxley deliver the contemptuous 'Spare us — the brats of Mudbloods do not stir our sympathies' line directly in the courtroom.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Yaxley is present on the platform but is entirely silent throughout the hearing. He has no lines, no jeering laugh, no ideological contribution. When Umbridge is stunned, 'Ron is too quick and takes him out with a single blast' — his neutralisation is handled by Ron rather than Harry, and it is instantaneous with no attempt by Yaxley to respond. His courtroom line ('Spare us') is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book positions Yaxley as an active ideological participant in the hearing, not a mute presence. His jeering laugh and his 'brats of Mudbloods' line demonstrate that he is an enthusiastic enforcer of blood-purity law, not merely Umbridge's security detail. The film renders him entirely passive, and his defeat is handed to Ron rather than Harry, which is a minor reassignment of agency. Together these choices reduce a characterised scene participant to a prop that needs to be dealt with before the trio can escape.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Atrium escape / Grimmauld Place breach
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Yaxley recovers and bursts from a lift shouting 'Seal the exit! SEAL IT!', Harry punches the balding wizard and shouts a deflecting lie ('He's been helping Muggle-borns escape, Yaxley!'), Yaxley is momentarily confused looking between Harry and the punched wizard, then Harry sees 'an inkling of truth dawn on that brutish face.' Yaxley then pursues through the fireplace, grabs Hermione's sleeve during Disapparition, and is taken to the threshold of Grimmauld Place — a plot-critical act with lasting consequences for the entire camping arc.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Yaxley staggers in shouting 'Seal the exits! Now!', fires on the trio as fireplaces seal one by one, and physically dives into the last fireplace just before it seals — catching hold of Hermione in the whirlwind. The book's moment of Yaxley being deceived by Harry's shout (the 'inkling of truth' beat) is absent. The mechanics are simplified: he is not confused, just physically pursuing. The Grimmauld Place breach consequence is preserved in the aftermath scene (Hermione's explanation in the forest).
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's brief beat where Harry successfully misdirects Yaxley with a lie — and Yaxley is nearly taken in before his instincts kick in — gives the character a moment of being outmanoeuvred by Harry's quick thinking, which is a small but satisfying payoff to Yaxley's established shrewdness. The film replaces this with a purely physical chase. The loss is minor given that the plot consequence (Grimmauld Place breach) is fully preserved, but the characterisation beat is gone.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Forbidden Forest clearing (Harry's walk to death)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Yaxley and Dolohov patrol the forest together, speculating whether Harry will come ('Time's nearly up. Porter's had his hour. He's not coming.' / 'Better go back. Find out what the plan is now.'), and Yaxley then leads Harry — unwittingly — to the clearing. Yaxley is a named, speaking participant in the forest vigil who comments on Hagrid's creature-keeping and checks his watch, present as a recognisable antagonist at this climactic moment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Yaxley enters the clearing and reports 'No sign of him, my Lord.' He then silences Hagrid with a wand-flick when Hagrid cries out at Harry's arrival. These are his only contributions. The patrol conversation with Dolohov in the forest is absent; Yaxley simply appears at the clearing having evidently been searching.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The forest patrol scene is compressed, which is unsurprising for a climactic sequence. Yaxley's lines in the book give him a workmanlike, pragmatic presence even at the saga's most charged moment. The film retains him as a named actor who silences Hagrid — a small but visible action — so the loss is limited. Confidence in this entry is medium since the compression serves pacing rather than representing a characterisation choice.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Battle of Hogwarts (Great Hall)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Yaxley is 'slammed to the floor by George and Lee Jordan' in the Great Hall during the final battle — a specific, named defeat that gives him a clear endpoint and ties him to named heroes.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus does not contain any scene showing Yaxley's defeat in the Battle of Hogwarts. He is last seen in the Forbidden Forest clearing. His fate in the battle is not shown or referenced in the available film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book gives Yaxley a named, satisfying defeat at the hands of George and Lee Jordan. The film omits this entirely — consistent with the general compression of the Battle of Hogwarts — leaving his fate unresolved on screen. This is a minor loss given Yaxley's secondary status, but it means the film provides no closure for the character who caused the loss of Grimmauld Place.
